title: SELECT Statement & Projections
description: Query relational tables, project specific columns, avoid SELECT *, compute expressions, and filter duplicates with DISTINCT and DISTINCT ON.

data.text: The **`SELECT`** statement is the primary retrieval command in SQL. It specifies the projection list (columns and expressions to return) and the data source (`FROM` clause).
Why You Must Avoid `SELECT *` in Production

data.title: Hidden Pitfalls of SELECT *
items: **Bandwidth & Memory Bloat**: Fetches wide columns (such as `TEXT`, `JSONB`, `BYTEA`) even if the application UI only displays an ID and a Name.
**Defeats Index-Only Scans**: PostgreSQL cannot satisfy a query using an index alone if columns outside the index are requested with `*`.
**Breaks Schema Decoupling**: If a new column is added or column order changes, brittle client applications expecting positional arguments will fail.

data.text: Standard SQL provides `DISTINCT` to eliminate duplicate rows across all projected columns. However, PostgreSQL offers an invaluable extension: **`DISTINCT ON (expression)`**. It retains only the first row of each group evaluated according to the `ORDER BY` clause.

data.title: Finding the Latest Order for Every Customer with DISTINCT ON
data.content: PostgreSQL's DISTINCT ON simplifies what would otherwise require complex window functions or correlated subqueries.
data.code:
-- Retrieve each customer's most recent order
SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id)
    customer_id,
    order_id,
    order_date,
    total_amount
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer_id, order_date DESC;

data.title: DISTINCT ON Rule
data.text: The leftmost expressions in `ORDER BY` must match the expressions inside `DISTINCT ON (...)` to ensure deterministic result selection.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Always project explicit columns instead of using `SELECT *`.
Use expressions and aliases (`AS alias_name`) to format result sets.
Use PostgreSQL's unique `DISTINCT ON (col)` to retrieve top-1 items per group effortlessly.
